description: A software engineer and a data scientist specializing in computer vision in the transportation industry.
summary: The Celestial Navigator app makes SPHEREx data accessible worldwide for anyone to observe and potentially discover astronomical objects. Users can examine well-studied areas such as the Pinwheel Galaxy or investigate their own area of interest. They can compare observations taken six months apart to track object movement, analyze differences in infrared brightness across wavelength bands, and assess emission and absorption features associated with certain chemical compounds. By automatically generating these time-based comparisons with easy-to-read visualizations and a user-friendly interface, the app helps curious users to explore space and uncover objects with distinctive features.
details:
This full-stack app (celestial-navigator-gs7y.vercel.app) analyzes and visualizes SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization, and Ices Explorer) data. It was developed using the React framework with TypeScript and Python. After a user selects a predefined or user-defined Right Ascension (RA) and Declination (DEC) position, cropped FITS files associated with that location are ingested. These include data from different available detector bands (e.g., D1, D3, and D6) and time intervals. False colours are assigned to each detector band image and then combined to create an infrared composite image. These images ‘blink’ like a GIF across different time periods to make it easier to compare changes. There is also an image derived from calculating the difference in pixel values between two images of the same area derived from the same detector band but different time periods. An aperture spectrum is also created by summing the pixel values inside the circle at each wavelength and then subtracting an estimate of the background from the surrounding ring. This provides a heatmap-style view of the composite image. Similarly, spectral feature maps help identify areas with high levels of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAH), water, carbon dioxide, and carbon monoxide. PAH values are derived from measuring emissions from small carbon-based dust particles. The rest are derived from absorption dips in infrared light. 

The primary benefits of this app are the efficiently generated analyses of the changes in an area in space selected by the user. This project takes a creative approach that goes beyond tracking astronomical objects to include changes in light and chemicals. This is intended to make it easier for users to detect and uncover an area in space with unique astronomical features. We also added a map to make it easier for users to identify an area to select and explore. When a user selects a location, they receive progress updates on the data ingestion to align expectations and improve the user experience. We prioritized making the analyses easy to understand for anyone, regardless of their experience with space data. We also made this flexible so that future batches of data that update every 6 months can also be used for this app without us making additional changes.
